name: Decision-Making & Change
tagline: Choices, plans, advice and changing your mind
blurb: Eight cue cards drawing on one common stock of arguments. In terms of preparation time against likely return, this is the most efficient cluster in the entire 2026 forecast.

vocab.t: weigh up the pros and cons
vocab.def: to consider the advantages and disadvantages before deciding
vocab.n: Neutral and safe in all three parts. British English prefers weigh up; American English drops the particle.
vocab.eg: I spent a fortnight weighing up the pros and cons before I turned the offer down.

vocab.def: to begin to doubt a decision you have already taken
vocab.vi: đâm ra do dự sau khi đã quyết
vocab.n: The doubt follows the decision — that sequence is what the phrase encodes, and using it before a decision is a common error.
vocab.eg: I had already signed the contract when I started having second thoughts.

vocab.def: to decide on instinct rather than analysis
vocab.n: Informal. The more formal equivalent, trust my instincts, is preferable if the surrounding register is measured.
vocab.eg: There wasn't time to research it properly, so I went with my gut and never regretted it.

vocab.def: to postpone a decision until the following day
vocab.n: Highly idiomatic and genuinely common in everyday speech, which is what gives it value in Part 1.
vocab.eg: My father's advice was always to sleep on any decision involving money.

vocab.def: a decision taken in the absence of adequate evidence
vocab.n: Slightly formal and strongly figurative. Reserve it for consequential decisions; applied to trivia it sounds inflated.
vocab.eg: Moving abroad at nineteen was a leap of faith, and it happened to pay off.

vocab.def: to withdraw from something you had committed to
vocab.n: Carries mild disapproval: the commitment was real and the withdrawal let someone down.
vocab.eg: He backed out of the trip two days before we were due to fly.

vocab.def: to discuss something in enough detail to resolve it
vocab.n: Positive. Distinct from talk about, which implies discussion without resolution — the particle carries the difference.
vocab.eg: Once we had talked it through properly, the decision more or less made itself.

vocab.def: judging with the benefit of knowing how things turned out
vocab.n: Almost always fronted, and ideally placed in the closing sentence of a Part 2 narrative. In hindsight is an accepted variant.
vocab.eg: With hindsight, turning that job down was the single best call I have made.

vocab.def: a reversal of opinion driven by feeling rather than by new evidence
vocab.n: More graceful than I changed my mind, and semantically narrower: the cause is emotional, not informational.
vocab.eg: She had been dead set against the idea, then had a complete change of heart overnight.

vocab.def: to be unable to choose between two things you want equally
vocab.n: Conveys genuine conflict rather than mere uncertainty. Followed by two noun phrases or two -ing forms.
vocab.eg: I was torn between staying somewhere safe and starting again from scratch.

vocab.def: a decision made suddenly, without prior thought
vocab.n: Informal and neutral in judgement; the surrounding clause supplies the approval or regret. Its opposite is a considered decision.
vocab.eg: It was a spur-of-the-moment decision and, frankly, a reckless one.

vocab.def: to act so as to destroy any possibility of return
vocab.n: Negative. Useful when discussing irreversible choices and the value of leaving options open.
vocab.eg: Resigning that way burned a few bridges I would rather have kept.

vocab.def: the paralysis that results from having too many options
vocab.vi: tê liệt vì quá nhiều lựa chọn
vocab.n: Academic and precise; a strong Part 3 item for questions about whether decisions are harder now than in the past.
vocab.eg: Choice overload is precisely why young people today find decisions harder, not easier.

vocab.def: to be undecided between two possibilities
vocab.n: British English. The American form is of two minds. Milder and more polite than torn between.
vocab.eg: I am still in two minds about whether it was the right thing to do.

vocab.def: to continue with something until it is finished, despite difficulty
vocab.n: Positive, with an implication of endurance rather than enthusiasm.
vocab.eg: Once I had committed, I was determined to see it through even when the funding fell apart.

vocab.def: to cause someone prolonged worry or guilt
vocab.n: Formal and emotionally serious. Suited to decisions with moral weight rather than practical inconvenience.
vocab.eg: That choice weighed heavily on me for months afterwards.

p1.q: Do you think you are an ambitious person?

b6.h: A position with a reason and an example
pts: Answer directly; do not open by repeating the question back.
One reason and one everyday example is enough at this level.
Keep to the present simple and resist drifting into a long anecdote, which belongs in Part 2.

b7.h: Define the key word on your own terms
pts: Separate the senses: professional ambition and personal ambition are not the same thing, and saying so is visible reasoning.
Add one less common item — set the bar high, quietly driven.
Close on a concrete detail that is demonstrably true of you.

b8.h: Take a stance towards the word itself
b8.f: Comment on the term → Admit a tension → Vivid proof → Short landing
pts: Remark on what ambitious connotes in your culture; the word is not neutral everywhere.
Acknowledge a contradiction in yourself. Slight self-deprecation reads as unrehearsed and confident at once.
End on a short clause after a run of longer ones. Rhythm is part of the assessment.

p2.q: Describe a difficult decision you made that had a good result

b6.h: Four prompts, two or three sentences each
b6.f: What → Why hard → What helped → Result
pts: Choose a decision that is easy to narrate: a school, a job, a move.
Hold the past simple throughout; unmotivated tense shifts are the commonest Band 6 error.
Aim for at least ninety seconds. Finishing under a minute is penalised even when the content is sound.

b7.h: Show the conflict, not only the outcome
b7.f: Two options → The pull of each → Turning point → Outcome → What it taught me
pts: Set out both options concretely so the listener can feel the weight of the choice.
Use was going to and had been planning to for the abandoned course of action.
Bring in a second person and give them one line of speech.

b8.h: Treat the decision as a collision of values
b8.f: Stakes → Competing values → Cost admitted → Outcome → Non-obvious reflection
pts: Show that the decision revealed who you are, not merely what you chose.
Admit what it cost. A narrative with no loss in it sounds invented.
Close with with hindsight, but say something that was not already obvious in the first sentence.

p3.q: Is it better to make decisions alone or ask for advice?

b6.h: Choose one side and support it
pts: State the position immediately.
Two supported reasons; balance is not required at this level.
Use I think or in my opinion, but not more than twice in one answer.

b7.f: It depends on X → Case A → Case B → Governing principle
pts: Divide by decision type: personal against professional, reversible against irreversible.
Raise the risk of consulting too many people, which most candidates overlook.
Finish on a principle rather than on an empty it depends.

b8.h: Ask what is being sought, and from whom
b8.f: Split the question → Name the paradox → Propose a test → Qualified verdict
pts: Distinguish asking for information from asking for permission; most people conflate the two.
Name the paradox: more consultation often produces less decisiveness, through choice overload and diffusion of responsibility.
Offer a usable test — has the person you are asking actually paid the price of a comparable decision?

critical.q: Is it better to make decisions alone or ask for advice?

for.main: An individual's judgement is distorted by biases that the individual is, by definition, not positioned to see.
sup: Blind spots. People systematically overrate their own capability and underrate risk. An outsider does not share that particular distortion.
Borrowed experience. Someone who has already made a comparable decision knows its real cost, which no amount of private analysis will reveal.
Forced articulation. Merely stating the problem aloud exposes the weak joints in the reasoning. The listener need not reply at all for this to work.

against.main: Advice is always offered from a position that does not bear the consequences.
sup: Misaligned incentives. The adviser does not live with the outcome and therefore tends to recommend what is safe for them rather than what is best for you.
Diffusion of ownership. The more people consulted, the weaker the sense of authorship; and when the decision fails, nobody learns from it.
Paralysis by input. Five conflicting opinions are worse than none. Consultation is often procrastination that feels like diligence.

critical.verdict: The Band 8 resolution: consult for the information you genuinely lack, not for the permission you already hold. The filter is simple — ask only those who have actually paid for a comparable decision.

models.q: Describe a difficult decision you made that had a good result
models.html:
I want to talk about a decision I made two years ago. I decided to change my major from business to computer science.

It was difficult because my parents didn't agree. They thought business was a safer choice and I would find a job easily. Also, I was worried because I didn't know anything about programming.

What helped me was my cousin. He works in IT and he told me the field was growing. I also did some research on the internet.

In the end, it was a good result. Now I enjoy my studies and I already have a part-time job. So I think I made the right decision.

notes.fc: Each paragraph answers one prompt in turn. The organisation is sound but the scaffolding is audible, and the opening formula announces preparation rather than thought.
notes.lr: Accurate but high-frequency throughout: safer choice, did some research, growing. No idiomatic item and no evidence of stylistic awareness.
notes.gr: The past simple is controlled and there are because and and clauses. No past perfect, no relative clause, no conditional.
notes.pr: Clear and easily intelligible, but the rhythm is flat and contrastive stress is largely absent.

models.prosody: I WANT to talk‿about‿a deCIsion / I made two years‿aGO ↘
models.tip: This runs to roughly fifty-five seconds. Part 2 requires between one and two minutes; falling short costs marks on Fluency and Coherence however accurate the language is.

models.q: Describe a difficult decision you made that had a good result
models.html:
Two years ago I did something my family still hasn't quite forgiven me for — I dropped business studies halfway through and switched to computer science.

What made it so hard was that everyone around me had a stake in it. My parents had been putting money aside for that degree since I was small, and business felt like the safe bet to them — something they could explain to relatives without a long conversation. Meanwhile I'd never written a line of code in my life.

The thing that tipped it was a weekend I spent with my cousin, who works in software. He didn't try to sell me on it at all. He just said, "Sit with the boring part for two days and see if you're still curious." I was, and that told me everything I needed to know.

With hindsight it was the best call I've made. I've got a part-time job now, and more importantly my parents have come round — though it took a full year and a very awkward Tết.

notes.fc: The opening is a dramatic detail rather than a formula, and transitions vary in function throughout. The long turn is produced without noticeable effort, which is the operative phrase in the Band 7 descriptor.
notes.lr: Have a stake in, the safe bet, tipped it, come round, the best call. Less common items appear naturally, and the line of direct speech brings a second register into the narrative.
notes.gr: Past perfect continuous, a relative clause, and extended compound sentences without error. A few sentences remain simple, which is what still separates this from Band 8.
notes.pr: Stress on hasn't quite forgiven creates the humour, and the falling contour on a very awkward Tết delivers the joke. Intonation is being used, not merely produced.

models.prosody: Two years‿aGO / I did something my family STILL hasn't quite forGIVen me for ↗ // I DROPPED business studies halfway THROUGH / and switched to comPUter science ↘
models.tip: Direct speech is the cheapest high-yield device in Part 2: it obliges you to change intonation, and the examiner hears phonological control immediately.

models.q: Describe a difficult decision you made that had a good result
models.html:
The decision itself took about forty seconds. Living with it took two years.

Halfway through a business degree my parents had scrimped for since I was six, I filled in a transfer form for computer science and handed it in before I could talk myself out of it. The difficulty wasn't the subject. It was that everyone I loved had quietly invested in a version of me that I was about to withdraw.

What actually settled it was a piece of advice so unhelpful it turned out to be perfect. My cousin, who's been in software for a decade, refused point-blank to tell me what to do. He said, "Spend a weekend on the tedious part. Not the exciting part — the tedious part." I did, and I was still interested on the Sunday evening, which frankly surprised me more than anyone.

The outcome has been good, though I'd be lying if I said there was no cost — there was a stretch of about eight months where dinner at home was distinctly chilly. What I took from it wasn't 'follow your passion', which I think is fairly useless advice. It was that the decisions worth making are the ones where you can't outsource the consequences — and if you can't outsource those, you probably shouldn't outsource the choice either.

notes.fc: Two short opposed clauses establish rhythm at once. All four prompts are addressed, yet none is visible as a prompt: topic development is coherent and appropriately extended rather than administered.
notes.lr: Scrimped, talk myself out of it, quietly invested, point-blank, a stretch of, distinctly chilly, outsource the consequences. Precise, idiomatic, and capable of dry humour.
notes.gr: Embedded relative clauses, a so … that construction with the conjunction elided, I'd be lying if I said, and a temporal where clause. Sentence shape changes with rhetorical function and errors are essentially absent.
notes.pr: The opening is a rhythmic exercise: parallel clauses with contrastive stress on FORty seconds and TWO years. The self-correction inside the quotation forces a mid-utterance intonation shift, and distinctly chilly falls into understatement.

models.prosody: The deCIsion‿itself took‿about FORty seconds ↘ ‖ (pause 0.5s) LIVing with‿it took TWO years ↘↘
models.tip: The half-second silence after the first sentence is the most valuable thing in the answer. Do not fill it with um. A deliberate pause counts as hesitation used to prepare content, which is a Band 9 feature rather than a fault.
